classification.difficultyReason: Apply signed multiplication and double-negative rules directly; repeated pronumerals become squares using the taught product rule.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a, b, d, e, g and h multiply signed coefficients and retain the pronumerals; c and f remove a double negative; i, j and k also combine repeated pronumerals as a square. Multiplication of algebraic terms is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 1 on PDF page 2 simplifies signed products, a double negative and a product containing two copies of the same pronumeral directly in one equality. The supplied continuation on PDF page 3 concerns Example 3 and is not needed for this question.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Simplify signed products and double negatives, including products of two algebraic terms.

classification.difficultyReason: Distribute the outside multiplier to both terms, tracking negative signs and fractional coefficients; no further algebraic procedure is needed.

questions.mappingNote: Question 2 requires only single-bracket distribution. Parts d, f, i–p and r directly assess negative multipliers; q applies the same method to a fractional multiplier. No collection of like terms or equation solving is required.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 recalls both distributive laws. Example 2 expands positive, negative and fractional multipliers by multiplying every bracket term; a minus before a bracket changes both signs. Page 3 continues Example 3 with expansion followed by collecting like terms.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand single brackets with positive, negative and fractional numerical multipliers.

classification.difficultyReason: Link distribution with collecting like terms, preserving signs and recognising when variable terms or the whole expression cancel.

questions.mappingNote: Question 3 applies this expand-then-collect method to one bracket with additional terms. Parts e, j and k include cancellation; parts e and g–l require careful treatment of negative terms.
questions.methodNote: Example 2 distributes the outside multiplier to each bracket term, including negative multipliers. Example 3 expands the brackets and then collects like terms; its solutions continue on page 3.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand one bracket and collect like terms, including negative multipliers and cancellation.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand two brackets, including subtraction of a bracket, then collect variable and constant terms.

questions.mappingNote: All twelve parts assess expansion of two brackets followed by collecting like terms. Parts e–l require distributing a negative multiplier, including an implicit multiplier of negative one in f and h.
questions.methodNote: Example 2 distributes positive and negative multipliers. Example 3c and d expand both brackets, reorder like terms, then simplify.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand two brackets, including subtraction of a bracket, then collect variable and constant terms.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose a common numerical denominator, rewrite the fractional terms, then combine signed numerators and simplify where possible.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly assesses addition or subtraction of algebraic fractions with numerical denominators. Parts a–d use equal denominators; e–t require common denominators, with j, k, m, n and p–t combining three terms.
questions.methodNote: Example 4 combines numerators over a common denominator, using the lowest common denominator when needed, and places a negative sign before the whole fraction. Example 5 reinforces collecting fractional like terms.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines two or three algebraic fractions using common numerical denominators, including subtraction and negative results.

classification.difficultyReason: Collect two sets of like terms using common numerical denominators, including negative coefficients.

questions.mappingNote: Page 4 explains common numerical denominators and Example 4 demonstrates algebraic fraction addition and subtraction. Page 5 Example 5 demonstrates collecting fractional algebraic terms. Question 2 applies these methods separately to the x and y terms; it requires no bracket expansion.
questions.methodNote: Use equivalent fractions with the lowest common denominator, combine numerators and collect like terms. Place a negative sign before the fraction when the resulting numerator is negative.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Collect two sets of like terms using common numerical denominators, including negative coefficients.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand signed brackets, identify fractional like terms separately from constants, and use common denominators to collect their coefficients.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts apply Example 5. Parts a and b combine equal denominators; c–f require equivalent fractional coefficients; d, f, g and h also distribute a negative multiplier. Page 6 confirms the printed Example 5 reference and that question 3 precedes the 11C boundary.
questions.methodNote: Page 4 demonstrates common numerical denominators and collecting fractional numerators. Example 5 on page 5 expands brackets first, combines fractional like terms using a common denominator, and leaves constants separate.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand positive and negative multipliers, then combine fractional coefficients and constants.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand positive and negative multipliers, then combine algebraic terms and exact fractional constants, including a mixed number.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts follow Example 5's expansion-then-collection sequence. Parts a–c use positive multipliers; d–e distribute a negative multiplier; f multiplies a negative algebraic term. Fractional constants are combined exactly, e converts the mixed number to 9/2, and d's algebraic terms cancel. The question lies above the 11C band and remains Exercise 11B.
questions.methodNote: Page 4 establishes common-denominator addition and subtraction and placing a negative sign before the entire fraction. Example 5 on page 5 expands brackets first, collects fractional like terms using a common denominator, then simplifies. Pages 6–7 introduce the following equations topic; its inverse-operation methods are not needed here.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand positive and negative multipliers, then combine algebraic terms and exact fractional constants, including a mixed number.

classification.difficultyReason: Select and apply the taught inverse operations, undoing the constant before the coefficient in two-step equations and handling signed division.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c undo addition or subtraction; d–f divide by the signed coefficient; g multiplies by 5; h multiplies by 2 then divides by −5; i–l remove the constant then divide by the signed coefficient. All follow the valid routes of Example 6. Neither reuse candidate matches the complete twelve-part task.
questions.methodNote: Example 6 teaches applying the same inverse operation to both sides, removing an additive constant before dividing by the coefficient, and retaining exact mixed-number results. Its direct division route is valid; the alternative route in 6(b) has an incorrect printed negative divisor and is not used. Example 7(b) changes variable between prompt and working; Example 8(a) prints 240 in a substitution numerator instead of 420. These excluded discrepancies are preserved as evidence and do not affect the selected method.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply one or two inverse operations, including division by negative coefficients and exact fractional answers.

classification.difficultyReason: Collect terms, expand brackets where needed and solve, including equations with pronumerals on both sides.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c collect terms; d–f expand and collect; g–l gather pronumerals; m–p combine gathering with expansion or a numerical fraction. Neither reuse candidate matches the complete sixteen-part task.
questions.methodNote: Examples 6–7 collect like terms, expand brackets and apply the same inverse operation to both sides. Example 7 gathers pronumeral terms to retain a positive coefficient; page 8 also establishes clearing numerical denominators.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Collect terms, expand brackets where needed and solve, including equations with pronumerals on both sides.

classification.difficultyReason: Undo a constant operation and numerical fractional coefficient, including a negative coefficient.

questions.mappingNote: Each part has one algebraic fraction and a constant; remove the constant, clear the denominator and divide by the coefficient.
questions.methodNote: Example 6 uses inverse operations on both sides, including division by a negative coefficient; pages 8–9 establish multiplying both sides by numerical denominators.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Undo a constant operation and numerical fractional coefficient, including a negative coefficient.

classification.difficultyReason: Clear multiple numerical denominators, collect terms and solve; later parts include brackets or an additional constant.

questions.mappingNote: All parts use the demonstrated denominator-clearing method. Part k first divides both sides by 3; part l first subtracts 12. Four source columns are reduced to three for fraction readability and handwriting.
questions.methodNote: Page 8 Method 2 and page 9 Example 8 multiply both sides by the lowest common multiple of numerical denominators, then collect terms and divide by the coefficient.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Clear multiple numerical denominators, collect terms and solve; later parts include brackets or an additional constant.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise a contradiction after eliminating the pronumeral and explain why no solution exists.

questions.mappingNote: The task directly assesses recognising a contradiction; the algebra and answer agree with the teacher key, but explicit original teaching evidence for this dependency remains required.
questions.methodNote: Example 7 supports subtracting the same pronumeral term from both sides. The supplied teaching does not explicitly explain an inconsistent equation after both pronumeral terms cancel.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise a contradiction after eliminating the pronumeral and explain why no solution exists.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that both legs cover the same unknown distance, express their times as distance divided by speed, and equate their sum to 60 seconds before solving.

questions.mappingNote: The uphill and downhill legs share the same distance, so the Example 11 time-sum model applies directly. That explicit journey example occurs later in the chapter, and no claim is made that it precedes this exercise.
questions.methodNote: Pages 11–12 Example 11 defines one equal journey distance, expresses each time as distance divided by speed, adds the times and clears numerical denominators. Pages 8–9 establish the fractional-equation operations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Model two journey times using the same unknown distance, add them and solve a fractional equation.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate verbal operations into equations, preserving bracket grouping and subtraction order, then clear denominators or gather unknown terms as required.

questions.mappingNote: Part a translates successive operations into a bracketed equation; b and c model sums of fractional portions; d preserves the stated subtraction order; e equates two expressions and gathers unknown terms with a positive coefficient. Equation modelling is the shared assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 9 translates a number problem into an equation and uses balanced inverse operations. Pages 8–9 teach clearing numerical denominators by their lowest common multiple. Examples 6–7 teach inverse operations and collecting unknown terms on one side.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate verbal operations into equations, including subtraction order, fractional coefficients and an unknown on both sides.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate verbal operations into equations, preserving subtraction order and grouping, then solve using inverse operations.

questions.mappingNote: Each part assesses equation formation from words. Part a subtracts two fractions of the same unknown; b groups the subtraction before multiplication by −5; c adds 6 to two-thirds of the unknown; d subtracts the constant two-thirds from half the unknown. These distinctions determine the equations and are preserved.
questions.methodNote: Example 9 defines an unknown, translates the verbal relationship into an equation and solves by inverse operations. Pages 6–8 demonstrate negative coefficients and clearing numerical denominators; Example 10 and the continuation of Example 11 reinforce forming and solving equations containing fractions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate verbal operations into equations, preserving subtraction order and grouping, then solve using inverse operations.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert each price and shared mass into a cost term, add the costs to match the total, and solve the resulting single-step equation.

questions.mappingNote: Question 3 applies the cost-modelling method of its printed Example 10 reference. Forming the equation from the purchases is the primary assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 10 on PDF page 11 expresses individual costs using one unknown, adds them to form the total-cost equation, collects terms and isolates the unknown. Examples 6 and 7 support inverse operations and collecting like terms.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Express two purchase costs using the same unknown mass, add them and solve a one-step equation.

classification.difficultyReason: Express the length in terms of the width, form a perimeter equation and obtain two exact fractional dimensions.

questions.mappingNote: Finding dimensions from a perimeter equation is the closest directly assessed skill. The supplied teaching supports equation modelling and solving, but does not explicitly establish the prerequisite rectangle-perimeter rule.
questions.methodNote: Examples 9–11 define an unknown, express related quantities using it, form an equation, solve using inverse operations and interpret the result. Examples 6–7 support collection of terms and division to isolate the unknown.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Express the length in terms of the width, form a perimeter equation and obtain two exact fractional dimensions.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate a mean involving negative numbers into an equation and solve for the missing value.

questions.mappingNote: Question 5 uses this equation-modelling method with the prerequisite rule that the arithmetic mean equals the sum divided by the number of values. That prerequisite rule is not explicitly taught in the supplied context pages.
questions.methodNote: Examples 9–11 translate verbal relationships into equations, then apply the same operation to both sides to isolate the unknown. Example 11 clears numerical denominators before solving.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate a mean involving negative numbers into an equation and solve for the missing value.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert each set's sum and size into its mean, interpret the stated difference in the correct order, then clear denominators and solve for the possibly negative sum.

questions.mappingNote: The principal task is equation modelling: the smaller set contains eight numbers, so its average is x/8; the larger contains nine, so its average is 2x/9. The mean formula is a prerequisite not explicitly taught in the supplied chapter evidence.
questions.methodNote: Form an equation from the verbal relationship, following Examples 9–11. Clear numerical denominators using the lowest common multiple, as in page 8 Method 2 and Example 8a, then isolate the pronumeral.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate two averages into algebraic fractions and solve the resulting equation with a negative solution.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate a percentage of an unknown monetary amount and an additive comparison into a two-step equation.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed task is forming and solving an equation for an unknown monetary amount: ten per cent of m plus 500 equals 1280. Equation modelling is primary; percentages and two-step solving are supporting skills.
questions.methodNote: Examples 9 and 10 translate verbal relationships into an equation, apply inverse operations to both sides and interpret the result in context. The supplied teaching does not explicitly establish the prerequisite conversion of a percentage to a decimal multiplier.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate a percentage of an unknown monetary amount and an additive comparison into a two-step equation.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose the investment at 10% as the unknown, express the other portion as the remaining principal, and combine their percentage interests into an equation to expand and solve.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed task is constructing and solving an equation for two portions of a fixed investment. Equation modelling is primary; simple interest supplies the relationship used to construct the equation.
questions.methodNote: Examples 9–11 introduce an unknown, express related quantities using it, equate a sum to the given total and solve by equivalent equations. Examples 2–3 demonstrate expansion and collection of like terms. The supplied teaching does not explicitly establish the one-year interest rule required here.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Represent two complementary investment amounts using one unknown, form an interest equation and solve it.

classification.difficultyReason: Express both ages five years ago using the same unknown, then form and solve an equation.

questions.mappingNote: Express Anthony’s age as twice Julian’s age, subtract five from both present ages, and equate Anthony’s earlier age to three times Julian’s earlier age. Equation modelling is the directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 9 forms an equation from a verbal relationship and solves it by performing the same operation on both sides. Example 10 expresses related quantities using one unknown. Examples 2–3 demonstrate bracket expansion.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Express both ages five years ago using the same unknown, then form and solve an equation.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the taught equal-distance journey model, convert minutes to seconds, add the two half-journey times, and recover the full distance after solving.

questions.mappingNote: Question 10 has the same equal-distance, two-speed structure as Example 11, with speeds 4 m/s and 3 m/s and total time 35 minutes. Equation modelling is the primary assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 11 defines x as half the journey distance, uses time = distance ÷ speed, converts minutes to seconds, adds the two journey times and clears the numerical denominators before solving. Double x to obtain the whole distance.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Model equal journey distances at different speeds, convert minutes to seconds and solve the resulting equation.

classification.difficultyReason: Represent equal journey distances with one variable, add the two travel times and solve a fractional equation.

questions.mappingNote: Question 11 has the same equal-distance, different-speed structure as Example 11. Kilometres and hours already agree with the supplied speeds, so no unit conversion is required.
questions.methodNote: Example 11 defines x as half the journey distance, expresses each travel time as distance divided by speed, adds the times, clears denominators and doubles the solved half-distance.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Represent equal journey distances with one variable, add the two travel times and solve a fractional equation.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate fractional portions of one unknown into an equation, clear the denominators and collect pronumerals.

questions.mappingNote: Both fractional portions refer to the same number. Their sum equals that number plus 10, giving x/3 + 3x/4 = x + 10. Equation modelling is the primary assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Define the unknown and translate the verbal relationship into an equation, following Example 9. Clear numerical denominators by multiplying both sides by their lowest common multiple, following Example 8 method 2, then collect pronumerals and solve.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate fractional portions of one unknown into an equation, clear the denominators and collect pronumerals.

classification.difficultyReason: Express complementary angles using one unknown, translate a fractional comparison into an equation, and solve exactly.

questions.mappingNote: The main assessed task is constructing an equation from an angle comparison. Triangle angle sum supplies the second angle as 90-x, and clearing denominators permits the chapter's linear-equation method.
questions.methodNote: Examples 9–10 define an unknown, express related quantities using it, form an equation and solve using equal operations on both sides. Example 11 clears fractional denominators by multiplying both sides by a common multiple. Examples 2–3 support expanding brackets and collecting terms. The supplied teaching does not explicitly establish that the acute angles of a right-angled triangle sum to 90 degrees.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Express complementary angles using one unknown, translate a fractional comparison into an equation, and solve exactly.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the distributive law to a single bracket, including negative multipliers.

questions.mappingNote: Each of parts a–f requires distributing one numerical multiplier across two terms. Parts d–f specifically assess negative multipliers; no equation solving is required.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 recalls both distributive laws. Example 2 demonstrates expansion with positive and negative multipliers, including the sign change when multiplying a negative term.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the distributive law to a single bracket, including negative multipliers.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand positive and negative multipliers, then collect like terms.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts require expanding one bracket and combining the resulting terms with an additional term. Parts f–h specifically require a negative multiplier.
questions.methodNote: Apply the distributive laws, including the signs of negative products, then collect like terms as demonstrated in Examples 2 and 3.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand positive and negative multipliers, then collect like terms.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand two brackets, including negative multipliers, and collect like terms.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts apply Example 3c–d: distribute each multiplier, retain the resulting signs, regroup pronumeral and constant terms, then collect. Parts c and e–h directly assess negative distribution.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 recalls both distributive laws and demonstrates negative multipliers. Example 3, continued on page 3, expands both brackets, groups like terms and simplifies.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand two brackets, including negative multipliers, and collect like terms.

classification.difficultyReason: Select common denominators for up to three terms, convert their numerators consistently, and combine signed like terms into one fraction.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c use the equal-denominator procedure in Example 4a, with simplification in a and the negative-sign convention in c. Parts d–f follow Examples 4b–d using lowest common denominators 10, 20 and 21. Parts g–h extend the same procedure to three terms using denominators 12 and 30. Neither supplied reuse candidate has the same task or givens.
questions.methodNote: Page 4 introduces the lowest common denominator and Example 4 combines the adjusted numerators over that denominator, collects like terms and places a negative sign before the entire fraction. Page 5 continues combining fractional like terms.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine algebraic fractions using common numerical denominators, including three terms and negative results.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand positive and negative multipliers, then combine fractional like terms using common denominators.

questions.mappingNote: Part a directly follows Example 5a. Part b distributes 3 and reduces the resulting like fractions. Part c uses the negative-multiplier method before combining fifths. Parts d and f follow Example 5b with denominator 20; part e combines negative fractional terms with denominator 35. Neither offered reuse candidate matches this complete six-part task.
questions.methodNote: Examples 2 and 3 distribute multipliers, including negative multipliers, and collect like terms. Example 4 uses lowest common denominators to combine algebraic fractions. Example 5 expands brackets first, combines fractional like terms, and retains the constant separately.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand positive and negative multipliers, then combine fractional like terms using common denominators.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply one or two inverse operations in order; the hardest form requires removing a constant and then undoing a negative fractional coefficient.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–f follow Example 6a; g–j follow Example 6b; k–o, s and t follow Example 6d. Part p follows Example 6c. Parts q and r combine removing the constant with multiplication by the denominator, with r also using the negative-coefficient method of Example 6e. Neither supplied reuse candidate matches this complete twenty-part task.
questions.methodNote: Example 6 uses the same inverse operation on both sides: undo addition or subtraction, divide by a coefficient, or multiply by a denominator. Negative coefficients and exact fractional or mixed-number results are explicitly demonstrated.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use one or two inverse operations, including negative coefficients and exact fractional answers.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand or collect terms before solving, and gather pronumerals from both sides while retaining exact fractional answers.

questions.mappingNote: Part a follows Example 7a; b follows Example 7b; c combines negative distribution with Example 6b. Parts d, e, f, g, h, j and k gather pronumerals on the left as in Example 7c. Parts i and l gather them on the right to preserve a positive coefficient, as in Example 7d. Exact mixed numbers follow the source convention. Neither offered reuse candidate matches this twelve-part task.
questions.methodNote: Examples 1–3 establish sign handling, distribution and collecting like terms. Example 6 uses inverse operations on both sides and exact fractional answers. previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand or collect terms before solving, and gather pronumerals from both sides while retaining exact fractional answers.

classification.difficultyReason: Clear numerical denominators, collect variable terms and divide, retaining exact fractional and negative solutions.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts follow Example 8 method 2. Parts a, b and c clear their common denominators 7, 9 and 5 respectively. Page 10 Exercise 11C question 4 confirms that this method applies to both equal and unequal denominators. Neither supplied reuse candidate matches this complete six-part task.
questions.methodNote: Example 8 on page 9 explicitly teaches multiplying both sides by the lowest common denominator, then collecting terms and solving by inverse operations. It also demonstrates combining fractions first as an alternative. Exact answers are retained.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Clear numerical denominators, collect variable terms and divide, retaining exact fractional and negative solutions.

questions.methodNote: Example 10 models monetary relationships with an equation, solves using aligned algebraic steps and states the resulting cost in dollars.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate equal prize shares and individual profit into a two-step equation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Clear different numerical denominators containing binomial numerators, expand and solve exactly.
